query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying the Z method within ab initio molecular dynamics offers an efficient alternative to full thermodynamic integration for calculating melting properties (melting temperature, fusion entropy and enthalpy, and volume change at melting) in high‐melting refractory materials.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐melting refractory material in its crystalline (solid) state.
generation.intervention: Replace the expensive thermodynamic integration step in the ab initio free‐energy approach with the Z method simulation, in which the solid is overheated under constant-energy (NVE) conditions until it spontaneously transforms into a liquid.
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted at constant energy near the superheating limit, ensuring both the solid and liquid phases can be identified in the same simulation run.
generation.structural_mediator: The transition from a superheated (overdriven) crystalline lattice to a liquid state, which produces a discontinuous jump in energy and volume.
generation.mechanism: Under constant-energy conditions, the Z method drives the system into a metastable superheated state. Once a threshold energy is exceeded, spontaneous melting occurs; analysis of the energy discontinuity and volume change during this event yields the melting temperature, latent (fusion) enthalpy (and thereby entropy), and the volume change at melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Z method will produce melting property values comparable to those obtained from full ab initio free-energy (thermodynamic integration) calculations but with significantly reduced computational expense, making it more suitable for high-throughput screening of refractory materials.
generation.baseline: Conventional ab initio free-energy calculations using thermodynamic integration via molecular dynamics, which is highly accurate but computationally very expensive.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be valid for high-melting materials that do not exhibit extreme anharmonic behavior or complex multi-phase transitions at the melting point, where the assumptions of the Z method may break down.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative agreement between the Z method and full thermodynamic integration may vary with the complexity of the material’s chemistry and melting behavior; further, its reliability for highly compositionally complex alloys (e.g., certain refractory high-entropy alloys) remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of ab initio molecular dynamics simulations on a selected high-melting refractory material using the Z method. Initiate each simulation from the solid state under controlled constant-energy (NVE) conditions. Identify the spontaneous melting event by tracking abrupt changes in system energy and volume, and compute the melting temperature, latent heat (from the enthalpy jump), and volume change. Compare these results to values obtained independently from full thermodynamic integration (ab initio free-energy method).
measurements: Total energy and energy discontinuities at melting.
Volume changes during the melting transition.
Derived latent heat and computed fusion entropy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the melting temperature, latent heat, and volume change determined via the Z method significantly deviate (beyond a reasonably small error margin) from those obtained using the full thermodynamic integration method, or do not consistently reproduce these properties across multiple independent simulations, then the hypothesis that the Z method is a viable and computationally efficient alternative will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
